title: School Quality, Neighborhoods, and Housing Prices: The Impacts of School Desegregation
research_question: How do the characteristics of public schools to which a residence is assigned—such as student test performance and the racial and socioeconomic composition of the student body—affect the market value of single-family homes? To what extent does the apparent capitalization of school quality into housing prices reflect the schools themselves versus correlated neighborhood amenities and the endogenous sorting of households across neighborhoods?
data_description: The authors assemble parcel-level data on roughly 330,000 real estate parcels in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, from the county's Property Assessment and Land Record Management division, focusing on 89,793 sales of existing single-family homes (69,361 parcels) between January 1994 and December 2001, trimmed at the 1st and 99th price percentiles. Each parcel has precise geographic coordinates, structural characteristics (bedrooms, bathrooms, acreage, heated square footage, age, building quality grade), and tax-assessor neighborhood identifiers (1,048 neighborhoods). The Charlotte-Mecklenburg School District provided detailed elementary, middle, and high school attendance boundaries and school locations for 1993–2001. School-level data include student-level micro-data on math and reading scores in grades 3–5 (1993–1999), enabling computation of mean and value-added test scores, plus annual performance composites and demographics (1997–2001). Census block group data on race, median income, and public assistance from the 1990 and 2000 censuses are merged in.
institutional_context: Mecklenburg County, home of Charlotte, operated under a court-imposed desegregation order from the 1971 Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg decision through 2001. To integrate schools, the district drew attendance zones that frequently spanned non-contiguous, racially distinct neighborhoods, bussing students across the county and using satellite zones, mid-pointing, pairing, and magnet programs. A 1980 order required each school's Black enrollment to remain within 15 percentage points of the district average. Rapid population growth (36% in the 1980s, 26% in the 1990s) and rising minority enrollment forced periodic redrawing of attendance boundaries, especially when new schools opened: in 1997, two new high schools led to roughly 30% of residential parcels being reassigned, and in 1998 about 16–18% of parcels were reassigned at elementary and middle school levels. A 2001 appellate ruling ended race-based assignment beginning in 2002. This setting produces sharp differences in school assignment between nearby homes and substantial reassignments over time.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: RDD — treatment = neighborhoods with improved school quality, control = neighborhoods without change; cutoff = court-ordered desegregation

key_variables.treatment: improvement in school quality due to desegregation
key_variables.control: neighborhoods with no change in school quality
key_variables.time_period: several years before and after desegregation

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The main finding is that improvements in school quality due to desegregation led to an increase in housing prices.
